title: Θέτις καὶ Ἶρις ἄγγελοι
titleEn: Thetis and Iris Carry Zeus’s Word — Iliad 24.93–199
part: Thetis and Iris Carry Zeus’s Word (24.93–199)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Thetis takes a black veil and goes up from the sea to Olympus, where Hera gives her a cup and Zeus tells her why he has sent for her: for nine days the gods have quarrelled over Hector’s body, and some would have Hermes steal it, but Zeus will give Achilles the credit of returning it for a ransom. Thetis carries the message to her son, who is groaning among his companions, and tells him to give up the body. Achilles agrees if Zeus himself so wills. Zeus then sends Iris to Priam with instructions: he is to go alone with gifts, with only an old herald to drive the mule-wagon, and Hermes will escort him safely to Achilles, who will spare a suppliant. Iris finds Priam wrapped in his cloak and covered in dung, with his sons and daughters mourning around him; she calms him and delivers the message. Priam has the wagon made ready, goes down to his storeroom, and calls Hecuba to ask what she thinks.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα κάλυμμ’ ἕλε δῖα θεάων
κυάνεον, τοῦ δ’ οὔ τι μελάντερον ἔπλετο ἔσθος.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsasa kalymm’ hele dia theaōn
kyaneon, tou d’ ou ti melanteron epleto esthos.
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, she took a veil, heavenly-one of goddesses,
dark, and than it no garment was at all blacker.
sentences.i: With these words, heavenly even among goddesses, she took up a dark veil; no garment was blacker than it.
sentences.n: The subject is Thetis, who has just finished speaking in the last part (24.90–92); she is getting ready to leave the sea for Olympus. δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly even among goddesses’ is her epithet here. The Greek gives no reason for the black veil; readers usually take it as a sign of her grief for her son, but the poet does not say so. ἕλε is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’ without the augment (Attic εἷλε), and ἔπλετο is the epic ‘was’. κυάνεον ‘dark’ agrees with κάλυμμα ‘veil’, and μελάντερον is the comparative of μέλας ‘black’.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, πρόσθεν δὲ ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις
ἡγεῖτ’· ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα σφι λιάζετο κῦμα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
bē d’ ienai, prosthen de podēnemos ōkea Iris
hēgeit’· amphi d’ ara sphi liazeto kyma thalassēs.
sentences.l:
And she set out to go, and before her wind-footed, swift Iris
was leading the way; and around them the wave of the sea was bending aside.
sentences.i: She set out, and Iris, wind-footed and swift, led the way before her; and the wave of the sea kept swerving aside around them.
sentences.n: Iris, sent from Olympus at 24.77 to fetch Thetis, now leads her back. ποδήνεμος ‘wind-footed’ and ὠκέα ‘swift’ are her two stock epithets, here side by side. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘set out to go’, and ἡγεῖτ’ is the imperfect ἡγεῖτο ‘was leading’. σφι is the epic dative ‘for them, around them’. λιάζετο is imperfect: the sea keeps bending away on either side as they pass, a sign of divine passage that the Greek states without comment.

sentences.t: ἀκτὴν δ’ ἐξαναβᾶσαι ἐς οὐρανὸν ἀϊχθήτην,
sentences.tr: aktēn d’ exanabasai es ouranon aïchthētēn,
sentences.l: And having climbed up out onto the headland, up to heaven the two darted,
sentences.i: They climbed up out of the sea onto the headland and darted up to heaven,
sentences.n: ἀϊχθήτην is a dual, the Greek form for a pair, so ‘the two’ are Iris and Thetis. ἐξαναβᾶσαι is not a dual but a plural participle that agrees with the dual verb in sense; it is feminine because both are goddesses; ἀϊχθήτην is the passive aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’ with an active sense. ἀκτή ‘headland’ is where land meets the sea. ἐς οὐρανόν ‘to heaven’ is where Olympus is for this scene: the gods sit above the world, not on a mountain-top.

sentences.t:
εὗρον δ’ εὐρύοπα Κρονίδην, περὶ δ’ ἄλλοι ἅπαντες
εἵαθ’ ὁμηγερέες μάκαρες θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες.
sentences.tr:
heuron d’ euryopa Kronidēn, peri d’ alloi hapantes
heiath’ homēgerees makares theoi aien eontes.
sentences.l:
and they found far-thundering the son-of-Cronus, and around him all the others
were sitting gathered together, the blessed gods who are forever.
sentences.i: and they found the son of Cronus, who thunders from afar, with all the other blessed gods who are forever sitting gathered about him.
sentences.n: The son of Cronus is Zeus, named by his patronymic. εὐρύοπα is his stock epithet, translated by the traditional gloss ‘far-thundering’ even though its second half is disputed (it may come from ὄψ ‘voice’ or ‘eye, face’). εἵαθ’ is the epic third plural ‘were sitting’, and ὁμηγερέες ‘gathered together’ is the nominative plural. μάκαρες θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες is a formula for the gods as a body.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἄρα πὰρ Διὶ πατρὶ καθέζετο, εἶξε δ’ Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: hē d’ ara par Dii patri kathezeto, eixe d’ Athēnē.
sentences.l: And she then beside Zeus the father sat down, and gave way Athena.
sentences.i: She sat down beside father Zeus, and Athena gave way.
sentences.n: ἣ is Thetis. Athena ‘gave way’, presumably yielding the seat beside Zeus, though the Greek does not say whose seat it was or where she went; the courtesy shows how great an honour Thetis is given. εἶξε is the aorist of εἴκω ‘give way, yield’. Zeus is ‘father’ as the head of gods and men.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δὲ χρύσεον καλὸν δέπας ἐν χερὶ θῆκε
καί ῥ’ εὔφρην’ ἐπέεσσι· Θέτις δ’ ὤρεξε πιοῦσα.
sentences.tr:
Hērē de chryseon kalon depas en cheri thēke
kai rh’ euphrēn’ epeessi· Thetis d’ ōrexe piousa.
sentences.l:
And Hera a golden, beautiful cup in her hand placed
and cheered her with words; and Thetis, having drunk, held it out.
sentences.i: Hera put a beautiful golden cup in her hand and cheered her with words; and Thetis drank and held the cup out.
sentences.n: Hera is kind to Thetis, though at 24.55–63 she has just quarrelled with Apollo on Achilles’ side. The hand is Thetis’s, left to be understood. καί ῥ’ is καὶ ἄρα, ‘and so’, and εὔφρην’ is εὔφρηνε ‘cheered’ with its last vowel elided. ὤρεξε is the aorist of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’; the Greek gives it no object or receiver, so ‘the cup’ is understood and who takes it is not said.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche patēr andrōn te theōn te·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the father of men and of gods:
sentences.i: Among them the father of men and of gods was first to speak:
sentences.n: This is a whole-line formula for the start of a speech, and the Greek is the same line as 22.167; the English is the one already published for it. μύθων ἦρχε takes the genitive: ‘began (made a beginning of) speeches’. The father of men and of gods is Zeus, and the speech that follows is his to Thetis.

sentences.t:
ἤλυθες Οὔλυμπον δὲ θεὰ Θέτι κηδομένη περ,
πένθος ἄλαστον ἔχουσα μετὰ φρεσίν· οἶδα καὶ αὐτός·
sentences.tr:
ēlythes Oulympon de thea Theti kēdomenē per,
penthos alaston echousa meta phresin· oida kai autos·
sentences.l:
“You have come to Olympus, goddess Thetis, grieved though you are,
having an unforgettable grief in your wits; I know it myself too:
sentences.i: “You have come to Olympus, goddess Thetis, worried as you are, with a grief you cannot forget in your wits; I know it myself:
sentences.n: Zeus speaks to Thetis kindly and at once names her grief. Οὔλυμπον δέ is Οὔλυμπον with the ending -δε ‘to’, so ‘to Olympus’, and Θέτι is vocative. κηδομένη περ is ‘grieved though you are’, and περ stresses that she is here in spite of her sorrow. ἄλαστον is traditionally ‘unforgettable’, though some ancient readers took it as ‘unbearable’, and its root is not certain. ἤλυθες is the epic aorist ‘you came’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ἐρέω τοῦ σ’ εἵνεκα δεῦρο κάλεσσα.
sentences.tr: alla kai hōs ereō tou s’ heineka deuro kalessa.
sentences.l: but even so I shall say for what reason I called you here.
sentences.i: but even so I will tell you why I called you here.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς is ‘but even so’: Zeus knows her grief, and yet there is a reason for the summons. τοῦ σ’ εἵνεκα is ‘for the sake of which’, a relative clause with the preposition after it; εἵνεκα is the epic form of ἕνεκα. ἐρέω is the future ‘I shall say’, and κάλεσσα is the aorist ‘I called’ without the augment.

sentences.t:
ἐννῆμαρ δὴ νεῖκος ἐν ἀθανάτοισιν ὄρωρεν
Ἕκτορος ἀμφὶ νέκυι καὶ Ἀχιλλῆϊ πτολιπόρθῳ·
sentences.tr:
ennēmar dē neikos en athanatoisin orōren
Hektoros amphi nekui kai Achillēï ptoliporthōi·
sentences.l:
For nine days now a quarrel among the immortals has arisen
about the corpse of Hector and Achilles, the city-sacking:
sentences.i: For nine days now a quarrel has arisen among the immortals about Hector’s corpse and about Achilles, sacker of cities:
sentences.n: This is the quarrel of the opening of the book, where Apollo and Hera took opposite sides. ἐννῆμαρ is ‘for nine days’, and ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι with a present sense, ‘has arisen and is still on’. ἀμφί governs both datives, νέκυι and Ἀχιλλῆϊ, ‘about’ the corpse and about Achilles. πτολιπόρθῳ ‘city-sacking’ is Achilles’ epithet here, in the dative.

sentences.t: κλέψαι δ’ ὀτρύνουσιν ἐΰσκοπον ἀργεϊφόντην·
sentences.tr: klepsai d’ otrynousin eÿskopon argeïphontēn·
sentences.l: and to steal him they urge the keen-sighted Argeïphontes;
sentences.i: and they urge the keen-sighted slayer of Argus to steal him;
sentences.n: The one they urge is Hermes, named only by his epithet ἀργεϊφόντης, traditionally ‘slayer of Argus’, though the meaning of the word is disputed. ἐΰσκοπον ‘keen-sighted’ is his other stock epithet. The Greek has no object for κλέψαι ‘to steal’: it is Hector’s body that is understood. ὀτρύνουσιν ‘they urge’ has no named subject; they are those among the gods who pity Hector.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τόδε κῦδος Ἀχιλλῆϊ προτιάπτω
αἰδῶ καὶ φιλότητα τεὴν μετόπισθε φυλάσσων.
sentences.tr:
autar egō tode kydos Achillēï protiaptō
aidō kai philotēta teēn metopisthe phylassōn.
sentences.l:
but I this glory to Achilles attach,
guarding for the time after your regard and love.
sentences.i: but I am giving Achilles this glory, keeping safe, for the time to come, my regard and love for you.
sentences.n: Zeus is saying that he will not let Hector’s body be stolen, and will let Achilles have the credit of giving it back. κῦδος ‘glory’ is what Achilles will win by returning the body for a ransom, which the following lines set out. προτιάπτω is προσάπτω, literally ‘fasten on’. αἰδώς ordinarily means ‘shame’, but here it is the regard that Zeus owes Thetis, and τεήν ‘your’ covers both αἰδῶ ‘regard’ and φιλότητα ‘love’. Here ‘your’ is taken as ‘toward you’, the regard and love Zeus has for Thetis, which is why the English says ‘my … for you’; the Greek could also mean the regard and love she has for him. μετόπισθε ‘afterward’ looks to the future: Zeus keeps the goodwill between them intact.

sentences.t: αἶψα μάλ’ ἐς στρατὸν ἐλθὲ καὶ υἱέϊ σῷ ἐπίτειλον·
sentences.tr: aipsa mal’ es straton elthe kai huieï sōi epiteilon·
sentences.l: Very quickly go to the army and to your son lay a charge:
sentences.i: Go at once to the army and give your son this charge:
sentences.n: αἶψα μάλα is ‘very quickly’, and ἐλθέ is the aorist imperative ‘go’. ἐπίτειλον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, lay a charge on’; the charge itself comes in the next lines as indirect speech. The army is the Achaean camp, and υἱέϊ σῷ ‘to your son’ is Achilles, with the epic dative ending -ϊ.

sentences.t:
σκύζεσθαί οἱ εἰπὲ θεούς, ἐμὲ δ’ ἔξοχα πάντων
ἀθανάτων κεχολῶσθαι,
sentences.tr:
skyzesthai hoi eipe theous, eme d’ exocha pantōn
athanatōn kecholōsthai,
sentences.l:
tell him that the gods are sullen at him, and that I above all
of the immortals am angered,
sentences.i: tell him that the gods are sullen toward him, and that I am angry at him above all the immortals,
sentences.n: What Thetis is to say is put as indirect statement: εἰπέ takes accusative and infinitive, so θεούς ‘the gods’ and ἐμέ ‘me’ are subjects of σκύζεσθαι ‘are sullen’ and κεχολῶσθαι ‘am angered’. The two verbs are different words for anger: σκύζομαι ‘be sullen, resent’, and χολόω ‘make angry’, from χόλος ‘anger’. κεχολῶσθαι is a perfect passive, ‘have been angered and am so’. ἔξοχα πάντων ἀθανάτων is ‘above all the immortals’. The unit ends in the middle of line 114.

sentences.t:
ὅτι φρεσὶ μαινομένῃσιν
Ἕκτορ’ ἔχει παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν οὐδ’ ἀπέλυσεν,
sentences.tr:
hoti phresi mainomenēisin
Hektor’ echei para nēusi korōnisin oud’ apelysen,
sentences.l:
because with raging wits
Hector he holds by the curved ships and did not release him,
sentences.i: because in his raging wits he keeps Hector by the curved ships and has not released him,
sentences.n: The reason for the gods’ anger: Achilles keeps the body he has been dragging. The unit begins in the middle of line 114. φρεσὶ μαινομένῃσιν is ‘with raging wits’, the dative of φρένες, with μαίνομαι ‘rage’ as at 5.185. νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν ‘curved ships’ is a stock phrase. ἀπέλυσεν is the aorist ‘released’, with ‘him’ understood; the Greek says ‘release’ and not ‘give back’.

sentences.t: αἴ κέν πως ἐμέ τε δείσῃ ἀπό θ’ Ἕκτορα λύσῃ.
sentences.tr: ai ken pōs eme te deisēi apo th’ Hektora lysēi.
sentences.l: in case perhaps he may fear me and release Hector.
sentences.i: in case he somehow fears me and releases Hector.
sentences.n: αἴ κέν πως is ‘in case perhaps, if somehow’, with an aorist subjunctive δείσῃ ‘may fear’ (δείδω). ἀπό … λύσῃ is one verb split by the particle θ’, ‘release’, the tmesis (separation of prefix from verb) usual in Homer. Zeus hopes that fear of him will move Achilles, which the following lines then make unnecessary: the gift of a ransom will do the work.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ Πριάμῳ μεγαλήτορι Ἶριν ἐφήσω
λύσασθαι φίλον υἱὸν ἰόντ’ ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.tr:
autar egō Priamōi megalētori Irin ephēsō
lysasthai philon huion iont’ epi nēas Achaiōn,
sentences.l:
But I to great-spirited Priam will send Iris
to ransom his dear son, going to the ships of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: But I will send Iris to great-spirited Priam, to ransom his dear son, as he goes to the ships of the Achaeans,
sentences.n: ἐφήσω is the future of ἐφίημι ‘send on’. λύσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of λύω, ‘to ransom, set free for a price’. The participle ἰόντ’ ‘going’ agrees with the unspoken subject of the infinitive, so it is Priam who will go to the ships, not the son. μεγαλήτορι ‘great-spirited’ is Priam’s epithet here, and Ἶριν is the accusative.

sentences.t: δῶρα δ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ φερέμεν, τά κε θυμὸν ἰήνῃ.
sentences.tr: dōra d’ Achillēï pheremen, ta ke thymon iēnēi.
sentences.l: and gifts for Achilles to bring, which may warm his heart.”
sentences.i: and to bring Achilles gifts that will cheer his heart.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Zeus’s speech. φερέμεν is the epic infinitive φέρειν, still part of what Iris will tell Priam. τά κε θυμὸν ἰήνῃ is ‘which may … his heart’: ἰήνῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἰαίνω, whose root sense is ‘warm’, so a gift that thaws or eases his anger; the English puts it as ‘cheer’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα,
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα,
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse thea Thetis argyropeza,
bē de kat’ Oulympoio karēnōn aïxasa,
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess Thetis, silver-footed,
and she went down from the peaks of Olympus, darting,
sentences.i: So Zeus spoke, and the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, did not disobey; she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus,
sentences.n: This is the formula for obedience: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘so he spoke, and did not disobey’, with the stock epithet ἀργυρόπεζα ‘silver-footed’ for Thetis. The second line is one already published in an earlier part, with the same English. καρήνων is the plural of κάρη ‘head’, here ‘peaks’, and ἀΐξασα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. The Greek does not name the speaker, who is Zeus.

sentences.t:
ἷξεν δ’ ἐς κλισίην οὗ υἱέος· ἔνθ’ ἄρα τόν γε
εὗρ’ ἁδινὰ στενάχοντα·
sentences.tr:
hixen d’ es klisiēn hou huieos· enth’ ara ton ge
heur’ hadina stenachonta·
sentences.l:
And she came to the hut of her son; there then him
she found groaning heavily;
sentences.i: She came to the hut of her son, and there she found him groaning heavily;
sentences.n: οὗ here is the possessive ‘her own’, from ὅς, and not the relative ‘who’: ‘the hut of her son’. ἷξεν is the aorist of ἵκω ‘came’, and κλισίη ‘hut’ is Achilles’ quarters in the camp. εὗρ’ is εὗρε ‘found’. ἁδινά ‘heavily’ is an adverb used with στενάχοντα ‘groaning’. The unit ends in the middle of line 123.

sentences.t:
φίλοι δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι
ἐσσυμένως ἐπένοντο καὶ ἐντύνοντο ἄριστον·
sentences.tr:
philoi d’ amph’ auton hetairoi
essymenōs epenonto kai entynonto ariston·
sentences.l:
and around him his dear companions
eagerly busied themselves and made ready breakfast;
sentences.i: and around him his dear companions eagerly busied themselves, preparing breakfast;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 123. ἐπένοντο is the imperfect of πένομαι ‘busy oneself’, with the augment. ἐντύνοντο is ‘were making ready’, and ἄριστον is the morning meal, ‘breakfast’. The picture is of a household going on with its day around a man who will not eat. ἐσσυμένως ‘eagerly’ is an adverb of ἐσσυμένος.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δ’ ὄϊς λάσιος μέγας ἐν κλισίῃ ἱέρευτο.
sentences.tr: toisi d’ oïs lasios megas en klisiēi hiereuto.
sentences.l: and for them a woolly, great sheep in the hut had been slaughtered.
sentences.i: and in the hut a great woolly sheep had been slaughtered for them.
sentences.n: τοῖσι is ‘for them’, the companions. ὄϊς is ‘sheep’ and λάσιος ‘woolly’, so a large fleecy sheep. ἱέρευτο is the pluperfect passive of ἱερεύω, which is ‘slaughter’; it may be a sacrifice but the Greek says only that the animal was killed for the meal.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ μάλ’ ἄγχ’ αὐτοῖο καθέζετο πότνια μήτηρ,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
hē de mal’ anch’ autoio kathezeto potnia mētēr,
cheiri te min katerexen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
And she very close beside him sat down, the lady mother,
and stroked him with her hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: She sat down very close beside him, his lady mother, and stroked him with her hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: Line 127 is a formula for a gentle address, found at 1.361 (Thetis to Achilles) and elsewhere, and its English is the published one. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is Thetis, and αὐτοῖο is the epic genitive of αὐτός ‘him’, governed by ἄγχι ‘near’ (here elided as ἄγχ’). κατέρεξεν ‘stroked’ is the aorist of καταρρέζω.

sentences.l:
“My child, until what point, grieving and sorrowing,
are you eating your heart, mindful of neither any food
nor bed?
sentences.i: “How long, my child, grieving and sorrowing, will you go on eating your heart, with no thought for food or for bed?
sentences.n: Thetis asks how long Achilles will go on without food or sleep. τέκνον is ‘child’, not ‘son’. τέο μέχρις is ‘until what point’, with the epic genitive τέο for τίνος. σὴν ἔδεαι κραδίην ‘you eat your heart’ is a figure for consuming grief, and ἔδεαι is the second singular of ἔδομαι ‘eat’. μεμνημένος takes the genitive and the negatives belong to it: ‘not mindful of food or bed’. ἀχεύων ‘sorrowing’ is a verb that goes with ὀδυρόμενος ‘grieving’. The unit ends in the middle of line 130.

sentences.t:
ἀγαθὸν δὲ γυναικί περ ἐν φιλότητι
μίσγεσθ’· οὐ γάρ μοι δηρὸν βέῃ,
sentences.tr:
agathon de gynaiki per en philotēti
misgesth’· ou gar moi dēron beēi,
sentences.l:
and good it is, even with a woman, in love
to mingle; for not for long will you live, for me,
sentences.i: and it is good to lie in love even with a woman; for you will not live long, as far as I am concerned,
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 130. Thetis tells him life must go on: ἀγαθὸν … μίσγεσθαι is ‘it is good to mingle’ (μίσγεσθαι is the Greek verb for sexual union, which the English puts as ‘lie’), and περ attaches to γυναικί ‘with a woman, even’, the Greek giving no name. The next words give the reason, that he has little time left. βέῃ is an epic future ‘you will live’, and μοι ‘for me’ is the dative of the person concerned, so ‘so far as I am concerned’. The unit ends in the middle of line 131.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τοι ἤδη
ἄγχι παρέστηκεν θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.
sentences.tr:
alla toi ēdē
anchi parestēken thanatos kai moira krataiē.
sentences.l:
but to you already
near has taken its stand death and strong fate.
sentences.i: but already death and strong fate stand close beside you.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 131. ἀλλά is ‘but’, and τοι is σοι ‘to you’. παρέστηκεν is a perfect, ‘has taken its stand beside and stands there’, with a singular verb for two subjects, θάνατος ‘death’ and μοῖρα κραταιή ‘strong fate’. Thetis knows from Achilles’ own destiny that he will die soon after Hector. Line 132 is also 16.853, said by Patroclus to Hector, and its English is the published one.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμέθεν ξύνες ὦκα, Διὸς δέ τοι ἄγγελός εἰμι·
sentences.tr: all’ emethen xynes ōka, Dios de toi angelos eimi·
sentences.l: But give heed to me quickly, and of Zeus, to you, a messenger I am:
sentences.i: But listen to me, and quickly: I am a messenger of Zeus to you.
sentences.n: Thetis opens her real message by claiming a messenger’s authority. ξύνες is the aorist imperative of συνίημι ‘take in, give heed to’, with the old spelling ξυν- for συν-, and ὦκα ‘quickly’ is an adverb. τοι is σοι ‘to you’. The same clause, Διὸς δέ τοι ἄγγελός εἰμι, is said again by Iris at 173, and has the same English in both places; it is also 2.26 and 2.63, with the same English.

sentences.t:
σκύζεσθαι σοί φησι θεούς, ἑὲ δ’ ἔξοχα πάντων
ἀθανάτων κεχολῶσθαι,
sentences.tr:
skyzesthai soi phēsi theous, hee d’ exocha pantōn
athanatōn kecholōsthai,
sentences.l:
he says that the gods are sullen at you, and that he himself above all
of the immortals is angered,
sentences.i: He says that the gods are sullen toward you, and that he himself is angry at you above all the immortals,
sentences.n: This repeats Zeus’s own words to Thetis (113–114), with the persons changed for Thetis to say them to Achilles. φησί introduces accusative and infinitive, with θεούς and ἑὲ ‘him’ as subjects; ἑέ is the accusative of the pronoun, ‘him, himself’, so Zeus. σκύζεσθαι is ‘be sullen’ and κεχολῶσθαι ‘be angered’, as before. The unit ends in the middle of line 135.

sentences.t:
ὅτι φρεσὶ μαινομένῃσιν
Ἕκτορ’ ἔχεις παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν οὐδ’ ἀπέλυσας.
sentences.tr:
hoti phresi mainomenēisin
Hektor’ echeis para nēusi korōnisin oud’ apelysas.
sentences.l:
because with raging wits
Hector you hold by the curved ships and did not release him.
sentences.i: because in your raging wits you keep Hector by the curved ships and have not released him.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 135. This is line 115 with the verbs in the second person, ἔχεις ‘you hold’ and ἀπέλυσας ‘you released’, the same Greek and the same English apart from the person. φρεσὶ μαινομένῃσιν ‘with raging wits’ is the dative of φρένες.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ λῦσον, νεκροῖο δὲ δέξαι ἄποινα.
sentences.tr: all’ age dē lyson, nekroio de dexai apoina.
sentences.l: But come now, release him, and for the corpse accept ransom.”
sentences.i: So come now, release him, and accept ransom for the corpse.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Thetis’s speech. ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’. λῦσον is the aorist imperative of λύω ‘release’, with the body understood. δέξαι is the aorist middle imperative of δέχομαι ‘accept’. νεκροῖο is the epic genitive of νεκρός ‘corpse’, with ἄποινα ‘ransom’ as the price for it.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to her:
sentences.n: This is the whole-line formula for a reply, the same Greek as in earlier parts, and its English is the one already published. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift of foot’ is Achilles’ stock epithet, with πόδας an accusative of respect. ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι.

sentences.t:
τῇδ’ εἴη· ὃς ἄποινα φέροι καὶ νεκρὸν ἄγοιτο,
εἰ δὴ πρόφρονι θυμῷ Ὀλύμπιος αὐτὸς ἀνώγει.
sentences.tr:
tēid’ eiē· hos apoina pheroi kai nekron agoito,
ei dē prophroni thymōi Olympios autos anōgei.
sentences.l:
“Thus let it be: let him who brings ransom also take away the corpse,
if indeed with a ready-minded heart the Olympian himself bids it.”
sentences.i: “So be it: let him who brings ransom take the corpse away, if the Olympian himself truly bids it with a ready heart.”
sentences.n: Achilles gives in at once, and in two lines. τῇδ’ εἴη is ‘thus let it be’, with an optative of wish; ὃς ἄποινα φέροι καὶ νεκρὸν ἄγοιτο is a relative clause in the optative, ‘whoever brings ransom, let him take away the corpse’. ἄγοιτο is middle: ‘take for himself’. εἰ δὴ … ἀνώγει ‘if indeed he bids’ is a plain condition with the indicative, ‘if he really does bid it’. ‘The Olympian himself’ is Zeus. πρόφρονι is ‘ready-minded’ and θυμῷ ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἵ γ’ ἐν νηῶν ἀγύρει μήτηρ τε καὶ υἱὸς
πολλὰ πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευον.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi g’ en nēōn agyrei mētēr te kai huios
polla pros allēlous epea pteroent’ agoreuon.
sentences.l:
So they in the gathering of the ships, mother and son,
many winged words to one another spoke.
sentences.i: So, in the throng of the ships, mother and son spoke many winged words to one another.
sentences.n: This closes the scene in the camp. ἀγύρει is the dative of ἀγύρις ‘gathering’ (‘throng’ in the English), here the crowd of ships drawn up on the beach; that is, among the ships of the camp. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase for spoken words, and here ἀγόρευον ‘spoke’ is plural because the subject is both mother and son. ἀλλήλους ‘one another’ is the reciprocal pronoun.

sentences.t: Ἶριν δ’ ὄτρυνε Κρονίδης εἰς Ἴλιον ἱρήν·
sentences.tr: Irin d’ otryne Kronidēs eis Ilion hirēn·
sentences.l: And Iris the son-of-Cronus urged on to sacred Ilium:
sentences.i: And the son of Cronus urged Iris on to sacred Ilium:
sentences.n: The scene changes to Olympus, though the Greek does not say ‘meanwhile’. Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus, and Ἶριν is the object, so Iris is the one sent. ὄτρυνε ‘urged on’ is the aorist of ὀτρύνω. Ἴλιον ἱρήν ‘sacred Ilium’ is a stock phrase for Troy.

sentences.t:
βάσκ’ ἴθι Ἶρι ταχεῖα λιποῦσ’ ἕδος Οὐλύμποιο
ἄγγειλον Πριάμῳ μεγαλήτορι Ἴλιον εἴσω
λύσασθαι φίλον υἱὸν ἰόντ’ ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν,
δῶρα δ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ φερέμεν τά κε θυμὸν ἰήνῃ
οἶον, μὴ δέ τις ἄλλος ἅμα Τρώων ἴτω ἀνήρ.
sentences.tr:
bask’ ithi Iri tacheia lipous’ hedos Oulympoio
angeilon Priamōi megalētori Ilion eisō
lysasthai philon huion iont’ epi nēas Achaiōn,
dōra d’ Achillēï pheremen ta ke thymon iēnēi
oion, mē de tis allos hama Trōōn itō anēr.
sentences.l:
“Go, set out, swift Iris, having left the seat of Olympus,
announce to great-spirited Priam within Ilium
to ransom his dear son, going to the ships of the Achaeans,
and gifts for Achilles to bring, which may warm his heart,
alone; and let no other man of the Trojans go along.
sentences.i: “Be off with you, swift Iris, leaving the seat of Olympus, and bring word to great-spirited Priam inside Ilium, to ransom his dear son, as he goes to the ships of the Achaeans, and to bring Achilles gifts that will cheer his heart, himself alone; let no other man of the Trojans go with him.
sentences.n: Zeus gives the commission to Iris. βάσκ’ ἴθι is two imperatives together, ‘go, set out’, in a familiar order, and ταχεῖα is the vocative ‘swift’. λιποῦσ’ is the aorist participle of λείπω ‘leave’, and ἕδος is ‘seat’. ἄγγειλον is the aorist imperative of ἀγγέλλω ‘announce, bring word’. Ἴλιον εἴσω is ‘within Ilium’. The first two lines are lines 118–119 again, as Zeus told Thetis what Iris would say, and the English is the same. οἶον ‘alone’ is an accusative that goes with the unspoken Priam: he is to go alone. μὴ δέ is ‘and not’, and ἴτω is the imperative ‘let him go’. ἅμα is an adverb ‘along with him’.

sentences.t:
κῆρύξ τίς οἱ ἕποιτο γεραίτερος, ὅς κ’ ἰθύνοι
ἡμιόνους καὶ ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον,
sentences.tr:
kēryx tis hoi hepoito geraiteros, hos k’ ithynoi
hēmionous kai amaxan eÿtrochon,
sentences.l:
Let some herald, an older man, follow him, who may guide straight
the mules and the well-rolling wagon,
sentences.i: Let some older herald follow him, to guide the mules and the well-rolling wagon straight,
sentences.n: κῆρυξ is a herald, an attendant who carries messages and serves a great man; here an older one is to go as Priam’s driver, and γεραίτερος is the comparative of γεραιός ‘old’, ‘older’ than the others. ἕποιτο is the optative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, as a wish. ὅς κ’ ἰθύνοι is a relative clause with the optative, ‘who is to guide straight’. ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον ‘well-rolling wagon’ is the stock phrase; ἡμιόνους ‘mules’ is the accusative plural. The unit ends in the middle of line 150.

sentences.t:
ἠδὲ καὶ αὖτις
νεκρὸν ἄγοι προτὶ ἄστυ, τὸν ἔκτανε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
ēde kai autis
nekron agoi proti asty, ton ektane dios Achilleus.
sentences.l:
and also back again
might lead the corpse toward the town, him whom heavenly Achilles killed.
sentences.i: and who is also to bring the corpse back toward the town, the man whom heavenly Achilles killed.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 150. ἠδὲ καὶ αὖτις is ‘and also again, back’, and ἄγοι is the optative ‘might lead’, so the corpse is to be brought home by the herald. προτὶ ἄστυ is ‘toward the town’. τὸν ἔκτανε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς names the dead man by his killer, ‘heavenly Achilles’ being the stock epithet; ἔκτανε is the aorist of κτείνω.

sentences.t: μὴ δέ τί οἱ θάνατος μελέτω φρεσὶ μὴ δέ τι τάρβος·
sentences.tr: mē de ti hoi thanatos meletō phresi mē de ti tarbos·
sentences.l: And let not death at all be a care to him in his wits, nor any fear;
sentences.i: Let death be no care to him in his wits, nor any fear;
sentences.n: Zeus anticipates Priam’s terror. μὴ δέ … μὴ δέ is ‘and let not … nor’, with μελέτω the imperative of μέλω ‘be a care’. θάνατος is ‘death’ and τάρβος ‘fear’, and φρεσί is ‘in his wits’.

sentences.t:
τοῖον γάρ οἱ πομπὸν ὀπάσσομεν ἀργεϊφόντην,
ὃς ἄξει εἷός κεν ἄγων Ἀχιλῆϊ πελάσσῃ.
sentences.tr:
toion gar hoi pompon opassomen argeïphontēn,
hos axei heios ken agōn Achilēï pelassēi.
sentences.l:
for such an escort we shall give him, Argeïphontes,
who will lead him until, leading, he brings him near to Achilles.
sentences.i: for we shall give him such an escort, the slayer of Argus, who will lead him until, leading him, he brings him close to Achilles.
sentences.n: The escort is Hermes, again named only by his epithet ἀργεϊφόντης ‘slayer of Argus’ (the meaning is disputed). πομπός is ‘escort’, one who sends on his way, and ὀπάσσομεν is an aorist subjunctive that has the force of a future: ‘we shall give’, the gods acting together. ἄξει is the future of ἄγω ‘lead’, and εἷός κεν … πελάσσῃ is ‘until he brings near’, εἷος being ‘until’ and πελάσσῃ the aorist subjunctive of πελάζω.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ἀγάγῃσιν ἔσω κλισίην Ἀχιλῆος,
οὔτ’ αὐτὸς κτενέει ἀπό τ’ ἄλλους πάντας ἐρύξει·
sentences.tr:
autar epēn agagēisin esō klisiēn Achilēos,
out’ autos kteneei apo t’ allous pantas eryxei·
sentences.l:
But when he has led him into the hut of Achilles,
neither will he himself kill, and all the others he will hold back;
sentences.i: But when he has led him into the hut of Achilles, Achilles will not kill him himself, and he will hold back all the others;
sentences.n: The subject changes in the middle of the sentence: ἀγάγῃσιν ‘has led’ has Hermes as subject, but οὔτ’ αὐτὸς κτενέει has Achilles as subject (αὐτός ‘he himself’), the Greek giving no name, and the English supplies it. ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν ‘when’, and ἀγάγῃσιν is the aorist subjunctive. ἀπό … ἐρύξει is a verb split into ἀπό and ἐρύξει, ‘hold back’. κτενέει is the future of κτείνω.

sentences.t:
οὔτε γάρ ἐστ’ ἄφρων οὔτ’ ἄσκοπος οὔτ’ ἀλιτήμων,
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐνδυκέως ἱκέτεω πεφιδήσεται ἀνδρός.
sentences.tr:
oute gar est’ aphrōn out’ askopos out’ alitēmōn,
alla mal’ endykeōs hiketeō pephidēsetai andros.
sentences.l:
for he is neither senseless nor heedless nor an offender,
but very kindly a suppliant man he will spare.”
sentences.i: for he is neither senseless, nor heedless, nor a transgressor, but will spare a man who comes as a suppliant, and spare him very kindly.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Zeus’s speech to Iris, which began at 144. Zeus gives the reason why Achilles will not kill Priam. Two of the three words are rare and their meaning is not certain: ἄσκοπος is usually taken as ‘heedless’, and ἀλιτήμων as ‘offending, sinning’ against gods or men. ἄφρων is ‘senseless’. ἐνδυκέως ‘kindly’ is the adverb. ἱκέτεω ἀνδρός is an epic genitive, ‘of a suppliant man’, because πεφιδήσεται ‘will spare’ takes the genitive.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δὲ Ἶρις ἀελλόπος ἀγγελέουσα.
ἷξεν δ’ ἐς Πριάμοιο, κίχεν δ’ ἐνοπήν τε γόον τε.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, ōrto de Iris aellopos angeleousa.
hixen d’ es Priamoio, kichen d’ enopēn te goon te.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose up Iris, storm-footed, to tell the news.
And she came to Priam’s, and found shouting and lament.
sentences.i: So Zeus spoke, and storm-footed Iris set out to bring news. She came to Priam’s house, and found shouting and lament.
sentences.n: The first line is one already published in an earlier part, and its English is repeated. ἀελλόπος ‘storm-footed’ is Iris’s stock epithet; its second element is not quite certain. ἀγγελέουσα is a future participle ‘to tell the news’. ἐς Πριάμοιο ‘to Priam’s’ has ‘house’ understood. κίχεν is the aorist of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’, and ἐνοπήν ‘shouting’ and γόον ‘lament’ are its two objects.

sentences.t:
παῖδες μὲν πατέρ’ ἀμφὶ καθήμενοι ἔνδοθεν αὐλῆς
δάκρυσιν εἵματ’ ἔφυρον,
sentences.tr:
paides men pater’ amphi kathēmenoi endothen aulēs
dakrysin heimat’ ephyron,
sentences.l:
The sons, indeed, around their father sitting, inside the yard,
were soaking their clothes with tears,
sentences.i: His sons sat around their father inside the yard, soaking their clothes with tears,
sentences.n: Priam’s house in grief. παῖδες is ‘children’, but the sentence goes on to the daughters (166), so it is ‘sons’ here. ἀμφί goes with πατέρ’ ‘around their father’, and the father is Priam. ἔνδοθεν αὐλῆς is ‘inside the yard’. εἵματ’ ‘clothes’ is the object of ἔφυρον, the imperfect of φύρω ‘soak, drench’. The unit ends in the middle of line 162.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐν μέσσοισι γεραιὸς
ἐντυπὰς ἐν χλαίνῃ κεκαλυμμένος·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ en messoisi geraios
entypas en chlainēi kekalymmenos·
sentences.l:
and he, in the middle, the old man,
closely wrapped in his cloak, covered over;
sentences.i: and in the middle was the old man, wrapped close in his cloak;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 162. ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, and the verb ‘was’ is understood. γεραιός is ‘old man’, here Priam himself. ἐντυπάς is a rare adverb and its exact sense is not certain; the traditional reading is ‘closely, tightly’, so ‘wrapped close’. κεκαλυμμένος is the perfect passive participle of καλύπτω ‘cover’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ πολλὴ
κόπρος ἔην κεφαλῇ τε καὶ αὐχένι τοῖο γέροντος
τήν ῥα κυλινδόμενος καταμήσατο χερσὶν ἑῇσι.
sentences.tr:
amphi de pollē
kopros eēn kephalēi te kai aucheni toio gerontos
tēn rha kylindomenos katamēsato chersin heēisi.
sentences.l:
and around much dung
was on the head and neck of that old man,
which, rolling about, he had scraped together with his own hands.
sentences.i: and all around there was a great deal of dung, on the old man’s head and neck, which he had scraped together with his own hands as he rolled about.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 163. κόπρος is ordinary ‘dung’, the muck of a farmyard, and it is what a mourner heaps on his own head. ἀμφί is an adverb ‘around’. κεφαλῇ and αὐχένι are datives ‘on the head and neck’, and τοῖο is the demonstrative ‘that’ with γέροντος ‘old man’. καταμήσατο is the aorist middle of a rare verb, traditionally ‘scrape together’, and its exact sense is not certain. κυλινδόμενος ‘rolling about’ is a middle participle, and ἑῇσι is ‘his own’.

sentences.t:
θυγατέρες δ’ ἀνὰ δώματ’ ἰδὲ νυοὶ ὠδύροντο
τῶν μιμνησκόμεναι οἳ δὴ πολέες τε καὶ ἐσθλοὶ
χερσὶν ὑπ’ Ἀργείων κέατο ψυχὰς ὀλέσαντες.
sentences.tr:
thygateres d’ ana dōmat’ ide nyoi ōdyronto
tōn mimnēskomenai hoi dē polees te kai esthloi
chersin hyp’ Argeiōn keato psychas olesantes.
sentences.l:
And his daughters throughout the house, and his daughters-in-law, were grieving,
remembering those who, many and good indeed,
beneath the hands of the Argives lay, having lost their souls.
sentences.i: His daughters and his daughters-in-law grieved throughout the house, remembering those, so many and so good, who lay at the hands of the Argives, having lost their lives.
sentences.n: Line 166 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the scansion needs the syllable of ἰδέ before νυοί to count as long, as if νυοί began with two consonants, which it once did (νυός ‘daughter-in-law’), and the line ends in a spondaic fifth foot, with the υ of ὠδύροντο counted long. θυγατέρες ‘daughters’ and νυοί ‘daughters-in-law’ are joined by ἰδέ ‘and’, and ἀνὰ δώματ’ is ‘throughout the house’. ὠδύροντο is the imperfect of ὀδύρομαι ‘grieve’. τῶν is a demonstrative ‘those’, and οἳ δὴ πολέες τε καὶ ἐσθλοί ‘who were many and good’ describes the dead men. Line 168 is a line already published in an earlier part, and the English is repeated.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ παρὰ Πρίαμον Διὸς ἄγγελος, ἠδὲ προσηύδα
τυτθὸν φθεγξαμένη· τὸν δὲ τρόμος ἔλλαβε γυῖα·
sentences.tr:
stē de para Priamon Dios angelos, ēde prosēuda
tytthon phthenxamenē· ton de tromos ellabe guia·
sentences.l:
And she stood beside Priam, the messenger of Zeus, and addressed him,
uttering a little; and him trembling seized, the limbs;
sentences.i: The messenger of Zeus stood beside Priam and spoke to him in a low voice, and a trembling took hold of his limbs;
sentences.n: τυτθόν is ‘a little’, and with φθεγξαμένη ‘uttering’ it means that she spoke low or softly, so as not to terrify him more; the Greek does not spell this out. Διὸς ἄγγελος ‘messenger of Zeus’ is Iris. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’. τὸν δὲ τρόμος ἔλλαβε γυῖα is ‘trembling seized him, the limbs’: the person and the part affected are both in the accusative.

sentences.t: θάρσει Δαρδανίδη Πρίαμε φρεσί, μὴ δέ τι τάρβει·
sentences.tr: tharsei Dardanidē Priame phresi, mē de ti tarbei·
sentences.l: “Take courage, Dardanus’ descendant Priam, in your wits, and be not at all afraid;
sentences.i: “Take courage in your wits, Priam, descendant of Dardanus, and be not afraid at all;
sentences.n: Iris begins by calming him. θάρσει is the present imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’, and φρεσί is ‘in your wits’. Δαρδανίδη is a patronymic in the vocative, ‘descendant of Dardanus’, an ancestor of the Trojan royal house; it is not ‘son’. μὴ δέ τι τάρβει is ‘and be not at all afraid’, with the present imperative of ταρβέω ‘be afraid’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τοι ἐγὼ κακὸν ὀσσομένη τόδ’ ἱκάνω
ἀλλ’ ἀγαθὰ φρονέουσα· Διὸς δέ τοι ἄγγελός εἰμι,
sentences.tr:
ou men gar toi egō kakon ossomenē tod’ hikanō
all’ agatha phroneousa· Dios de toi angelos eimi,
sentences.l:
for not, indeed, I, foreboding evil, am I coming here,
but with good thoughts; and of Zeus, to you, a messenger I am,
sentences.i: For I do not come here foreboding evil, but with good thoughts; and I am a messenger of Zeus to you,
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τοι is ‘for indeed not’, with τοι as an address to him. κακὸν ὀσσομένη is ‘foreboding evil’, the verb of 1.105 (κάκ’ ὀσσόμενος), here singular and feminine; it is uncertain whether ὄσσομαι means ‘look at’ or ‘forebode’. τόδ’ ἱκάνω is ‘I come to this place’, and ἀγαθὰ φρονέουσα is ‘thinking good things’. The second clause is the formula of 133, Διὸς δέ τοι ἄγγελός εἰμι.

sentences.t: ὅς σευ ἄνευθεν ἐὼν μέγα κήδεται ἠδ’ ἐλεαίρει.
sentences.tr: hos seu aneuthen eōn mega kēdetai ēd’ eleairei.
sentences.l: who, though far from you, greatly cares for and pities you.
sentences.i: who, though he is far from you, cares greatly for you and pities you.
sentences.n: ὅς is the relative ‘who’, and refers to Zeus, named in the previous line. σευ is the epic genitive ‘of you’, and ἄνευθεν ἐών is ‘being apart from’. κήδεται is ‘cares for’ and ἐλεαίρει is ‘pities’, with ‘you’ understood for both. This line is also 2.27, with the same English.

sentences.t:
λύσασθαί σ’ ἐκέλευσεν Ὀλύμπιος Ἕκτορα δῖον,
δῶρα δ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ φερέμεν τά κε θυμὸν ἰήνῃ
οἶον, μὴ δέ τις ἄλλος ἅμα Τρώων ἴτω ἀνήρ.
sentences.tr:
lysasthai s’ ekeleusen Olympios Hektora dion,
dōra d’ Achillēï pheremen ta ke thymon iēnēi
oion, mē de tis allos hama Trōōn itō anēr.
sentences.l:
To ransom you bade, the Olympian, heavenly Hector,
and gifts for Achilles to bring, which may warm his heart,
alone; and let no other man of the Trojans go along.
sentences.i: The Olympian has ordered you to ransom heavenly Hector, and to bring Achilles gifts that will cheer his heart, yourself alone; let no other man of the Trojans go with you.
sentences.n: Zeus’s instructions of 146–148, now put to Priam directly, with the same English for lines 176–177. λύσασθαί σ’ ἐκέλευσεν is ‘he ordered you to ransom’: the infinitive is the aorist middle and σ’ is σε ‘you’. Ὀλύμπιος is ‘the Olympian’, and Ἕκτορα δῖον ‘heavenly Hector’. οἶον ‘alone’ agrees with the unspoken ‘you’.

sentences.t:
κῆρύξ τίς τοι ἕποιτο γεραίτερος, ὅς κ’ ἰθύνοι
ἡμιόνους καὶ ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον,
sentences.tr:
kēryx tis toi hepoito geraiteros, hos k’ ithynoi
hēmionous kai amaxan eÿtrochon,
sentences.l:
Let some herald, an older man, follow you, who may guide straight
the mules and the well-rolling wagon,
sentences.i: Let some older herald follow you, to guide the mules and the well-rolling wagon straight,
sentences.n: These words repeat 149–150 with τοι ‘you’ in place of οἱ ‘him’, and have the same English. The herald is to do the driving. The unit ends in the middle of line 179.

sentences.t:
ἠδὲ καὶ αὖτις
νεκρὸν ἄγοι προτὶ ἄστυ, τὸν ἔκτανε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
ēde kai autis
nekron agoi proti asty, ton ektane dios Achilleus.
sentences.l:
and also back again
might lead the corpse toward the town, him whom heavenly Achilles killed.
sentences.i: and who is also to bring the corpse back toward the town, the man whom heavenly Achilles killed.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 179. This is 150–151 over again, word for word. ἄγοι is the optative ‘might lead’ and ἔκτανε is ‘killed’.

sentences.t: μὴ δέ τί τοι θάνατος μελέτω φρεσὶ μηδέ τι τάρβος·
sentences.tr: mē de ti toi thanatos meletō phresi mēde ti tarbos·
sentences.l: And let not death at all be a care to you in your wits, nor any fear;
sentences.i: Let death be no care to you in your wits, nor any fear;
sentences.n: The same as 152 with τοι ‘to you’. The text prints μηδέ here as one word, against μὴ δέ at 152, and the sense is the same. μελέτω is the imperative of μέλω ‘be a care’.

sentences.t:
τοῖος γάρ τοι πομπὸς ἅμ’ ἕψεται ἀργεϊφόντης,
ὅς σ’ ἄξει εἷός κεν ἄγων Ἀχιλῆϊ πελάσσῃ.
sentences.tr:
toios gar toi pompos ham’ hepsetai argeïphontēs,
hos s’ axei heios ken agōn Achilēï pelassēi.
sentences.l:
for such an escort will go along with you, Argeïphontes,
who will lead you until, leading, he brings you near to Achilles.
sentences.i: for such an escort will go along with you, the slayer of Argus, who will lead you until, leading you, he brings you close to Achilles.
sentences.n: This is 153–154, with the escort now said to go along (ἕψεται, the future of ἕπομαι) instead of being given by the gods. Hermes is again named only by the disputed epithet ἀργεϊφόντης. ἄξει is ‘will lead’, and σ’ is σε ‘you’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ἀγάγῃσιν ἔσω κλισίην Ἀχιλῆος,
οὔτ’ αὐτὸς κτενέει ἀπό τ’ ἄλλους πάντας ἐρύξει·
sentences.tr:
autar epēn agagēisin esō klisiēn Achilēos,
out’ autos kteneei apo t’ allous pantas eryxei·
sentences.l:
But when he has led you into the hut of Achilles,
neither will he himself kill, and all the others he will hold back;
sentences.i: But when he has led you into the hut of Achilles, Achilles will not kill you himself, and he will hold back all the others;
sentences.n: This is 155–156 again, with the same shift of subject: Hermes leads, Achilles is the one who does not kill (αὐτός ‘he himself’). ἀπό … ἐρύξει is ‘hold back’ with the verb split by τ’.

sentences.t:
οὔτε γάρ ἔστ’ ἄφρων οὔτ’ ἄσκοπος οὔτ’ ἀλιτήμων,
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐνδυκέως ἱκέτεω πεφιδήσεται ἀνδρός.
sentences.tr:
oute gar est’ aphrōn out’ askopos out’ alitēmōn,
alla mal’ endykeōs hiketeō pephidēsetai andros.
sentences.l:
for he is neither senseless nor heedless nor an offender,
but very kindly a suppliant man he will spare.”
sentences.i: for he is neither senseless, nor heedless, nor a transgressor, but will spare a man who comes as a suppliant, and spare him very kindly.”
sentences.n: This is 157–158 again, with ἔστ’ for ἐστ’. As there, ἄσκοπος ‘heedless’ and ἀλιτήμων ‘offending’ are rare and not certain in meaning. The closing quotation mark ends Iris’s speech, which began at 171.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις,
sentences.tr: hē men ar’ hōs eipous’ apebē podas ōkea Iris,
sentences.l: She, indeed, then so having spoken went away, swift-in-feet Iris,
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Iris, swift of foot, went away;
sentences.n: This closes Iris’s speech and the scene. The line is already published in an earlier part, together with a different second line, and its English is repeated. ἣ μέν looks ahead to αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ in the next line, ‘she … but he’. πόδας ὠκέα is the feminine of Achilles’ epithet, ‘swift of foot’, here said of Iris. ἀπέβη is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω ‘go away’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ υἷας ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον ἡμιονείην
ὁπλίσαι ἠνώγει, πείρινθα δὲ δῆσαι ἐπ’ αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ huias amaxan eÿtrochon hēmioneiēn
hoplisai ēnōgei, peirintha de dēsai ep’ autēs.
sentences.l:
but he his sons the well-rolling, mule-drawn wagon
to make ready bade, and a basket to bind upon it.
sentences.i: but he bade his sons make ready the well-rolling, mule-drawn wagon, and bind a basket on it.
sentences.n: ὅ γ’ is Priam, and υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός. ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον ἡμιονείην is ‘well-rolling, mule-drawn wagon’; ἠνώγει is a pluperfect of ἄνωγα used for the past, ‘bade’. πείρινθα is a rare word whose sense is not known for certain: it is usually taken as a wicker basket or body that is fastened to the wagon, to carry the gifts. δῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of δέω ‘bind’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐς θάλαμον κατεβήσετο κηώεντα
κέδρινον ὑψόροφον, ὃς γλήνεα πολλὰ κεχάνδει·
sentences.tr:
autos d’ es thalamon katebēseto kēōenta
kedrinon hypsorophon, hos glēnea polla kechandei·
sentences.l:
And himself into the fragrant chamber went down,
of cedar, high-roofed, which held many treasures;
sentences.i: He himself went down into the fragrant chamber, a chamber of cedar with a high roof, which held many treasures;
sentences.n: Line 191 is also in the Odyssey, said of Menelaus, and its English is repeated from there. The chamber is Priam’s store-room, and κηώεντα ‘fragrant’ is the traditional gloss. κέδρινον ὑψόροφον ‘of cedar, high-roofed’ describe the chamber in the accusative. γλήνεα is a rare word whose meaning is not known for certain: it seems to mean something like ‘bright, precious things’, so ‘treasures’. κεχάνδει is the pluperfect of χανδάνω ‘hold’.

sentences.t: ἐς δ’ ἄλοχον Ἑκάβην ἐκαλέσσατο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: es d’ alochon Hekabēn ekalessato phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: and in he called his wife Hecuba, and spoke:
sentences.i: and he called his wife Hecuba in, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἐς … ἐκαλέσσατο is one verb split in two: ἐς means ‘in’ and the middle voice ‘to himself’, so he calls her into the room. Ἑκάβην is the accusative of Hecuba, Priam’s wife. φώνησέν τε is ‘and he spoke’, with the movable ν.

sentences.t:
δαιμονίη Διόθεν μοι Ὀλύμπιος ἄγγελος ἦλθε
λύσασθαι φίλον υἱὸν ἰόντ’ ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν,
δῶρα δ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ φερέμεν τά κε θυμὸν ἰήνῃ.
sentences.tr:
daimoniē Diothen moi Olympios angelos ēlthe
lysasthai philon huion iont’ epi nēas Achaiōn,
dōra d’ Achillēï pheremen ta ke thymon iēnēi.
sentences.l:
“Strange woman, from Zeus to me an Olympian messenger came
to ransom my dear son, going to the ships of the Achaeans,
and gifts for Achilles to bring, which may warm his heart.
sentences.i: “Strange woman, an Olympian messenger has come to me from Zeus, to ransom my dear son, as I go to the ships of the Achaeans, and to bring Achilles gifts that will cheer his heart.
sentences.n: Priam tells Hecuba what Iris has said; he does not name Iris. δαιμονίη ‘strange woman’ is the form of address, as Zeus used to Hera at 4.31, and its tone is not certain. Διόθεν is ‘from Zeus’ with the suffix -θεν ‘from’. Lines 195–196 are 118–119 again, with ‘my’ instead of ‘his’ for the son, since Priam now speaks of himself.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ τί τοι φρεσὶν εἴδεται εἶναι;
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe ti toi phresin eidetai einai;
sentences.l: But come, tell me this: what seems to you in your wits to be so?
sentences.i: But come, tell me this: what does it seem to you, in your wits, to be?
sentences.n: Priam asks for his wife’s opinion. τόδε εἰπέ is ‘tell me this’ and the question is τί τοι φρεσὶν εἴδεται εἶναι, literally ‘what seems to you in your wits to be’. The unspoken subject is the plan he has just described. εἴδεται is ‘seems’, the middle of an old verb meaning ‘appear’.

sentences.t:
αἰνῶς γάρ μ’ αὐτόν γε μένος καὶ θυμὸς ἄνωγε
κεῖσ’ ἰέναι ἐπὶ νῆας ἔσω στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ainōs gar m’ auton ge menos kai thymos anōge
keis’ ienai epi nēas esō straton euryn Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
For dreadfully, me myself, my might and heart bid me
to go there to the ships, into the wide army of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: For my very own might and heart dreadfully bid me to go there to the ships, into the wide army of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark ends Priam’s speech. αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’ marks how strongly he is driven. μ’ αὐτόν γε is ‘me myself’, accusative. μένος καὶ θυμός ‘might and heart’ are the two forces that drive him, and ἄνωγε ‘bids’ is a singular verb for both. κεῖσ’ is κεῖσε ‘to that place’, and ἔσω is ‘within’. στρατὸν εὐρύν ‘wide army’ is the camp of the Achaeans.
